notes: Hello everyone. Today, I will be presenting what I have been working on over the past few months.
I developed a surface grinding controller for a seven-degree-of-freedom Franka robot. The control method I used is Cartesian impedance control.

title: Motivation

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: TextBox 9
text: Grinding requires an aligned tool face.

shapes.name: TextBox 10
text: Calibration leaves uncertainty in the physical surface orientation.

shapes.name: TextBox 14
text: Cartesian impedance makes position and rotation compliant.

shapes.name: Passive contact alignment
text: Pressing a tilted tool creates a contact moment.

shapes.name: Compliance permits contact rotation
text: Rotational compliance allows the tool to turn towards alignment.

shapes.name: Joint friction orientation mismatch
text: Joint friction can prevent the desired tool alignment with the configured surface.

notes: Let’s dive into the motivation for this work. The main problem in surface grinding is that we cannot perfectly represent the real surface in our code and ensure that the configured and real surfaces are perfectly aligned.

Second, joint friction prevents us from achieving perfect alignment between the grinding tool and the configured plane. Because of these two problems, the tool first makes contact with the surface at an edge as it approaches.

The idea is to use impedance control, which, unlike conventional rigid control, allows the tool to respond to external forces and moments by making rotation compliant, for example. In this way, we can passively use the contact moment to bring the tool flat against the surface.

title: Cartesian impedance controller

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Decoupling statement
text: In the surface frame, K and D are diagonal and decouple translation and rotation.

notes: To understand the control method used here, impedance control uses a spring–damper model that produces a force to correct position and a moment to correct rotation. Together, the force and moment form what is called a wrench.
As we can see in the matrix form, force and moment are decoupled and do not affect each other when K and D are diagonal. K and D are the impedance parameters for stiffness and damping.
[Sources]

title: Translation–rotation coupling

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Coupling result
text: Non-zero off-diagonal blocks in K and D couple translation and rotation.

shapes.name: CoC position definition
text: Virtual centre of compliance (CoC): new reference

shapes.name: TCP reference definition
text: Tool centre point (TCP): controlled reference point on the EE

shapes.name: Reference point couples force and moment
text: Choosing an impedance reference point away from the TCP couples force and moment.

shapes.name: Virtual point force interpretation
text: The commanded force acts as if applied at the virtual point pc.

notes: An interesting idea presented in this work is to couple force and moment so that a pressing force also produces a rotational moment. This moment can either support or oppose passive alignment.

The idea is to choose a different reference point for the pressing force, moving it from the tool centre point to a point called the centre of compliance. This creates a lever arm that can produce an additional moment, which can either support or oppose alignment.
We transform the impedance parameters to this reference point so that the matrices now contain off-diagonal terms. This produces coupling between translation and rotation.
[Sources]

figures_and_images/sources/coupling_wrench_blocks.tex: the complete shifted wrench law. The underbraced matrices are A^T K_c A and A^T D_c A, expressed at the TCP in base-frame orientation.

title: Contact experiment

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Contact phases
text: Tool orientation    →    Surface approach    →    Contact establishment    →    Surface grinding

notes: Our contact experiment proceeds as follows. First, we orient the tool towards the configured surface and slowly approach it along its normal.
Once contact occurs, the tool aligns passively until it is completely flat. Grinding then begins along the tangential direction t₂.

To achieve this behaviour, we choose the impedance parameters as follows. For translation, we choose a compliant normal stiffness to allow pressing against the surface, while the tangential directions remain stiff to prevent unwanted movement during alignment.
For rotation, the normal direction is stiff, while the tangential directions are compliant to allow the tool to rotate.

title: Normal-force plausibility assessment

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

notes: Let’s first see whether our controller does what it is supposed to do. In this experiment, pushing the end effector about 20 mm along the surface normal, with Kₚ,ₙ equal to 1000, should produce a force of about −19 N in the quasi-static model.

We can see in the plot that the mean commanded force is close to the quasi-static prediction because our motion is very slow and almost static. For the model estimate, which serves as our measurement here, the difference also remains small, at about 13 percent.

title: Commanded and estimated wrench

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

notes: Next, we compare the commanded force and moment with the measurements during contact. At first, as the tool approaches the surface, the model cannot measure anything because of friction, and motion begins only after a certain force is reached.
The force then starts to ramp down until contact occurs at around 0.4 seconds, where we can see this jump. The tool then starts aligning, with force and moment changing linearly.

Once the tool is flat, the force and moment become stationary, and the measurement is exactly equal to the command. For the moment, we also observe a larger gap between the estimated and commanded values during alignment.
This proves that alignment occurs through an external contact moment and is achieved passively.

title: Effect of CoC position

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

notes: Next, this plot shows how the centre of compliance affects the final error. We moved the centre of compliance from −80 to +80 mm for two starting rotations, +10 and −10 degrees.

Looking at the blue curve for the −10-degree rotation, a negative centre-of-compliance displacement supports alignment, and the tool ends up approximately flat, with an error of about 2 degrees. The error becomes smaller as the displacement approaches zero, after which it becomes progressively worse.

For the black curve, with a +10-degree starting rotation, the tool remains flat until the displacement reaches about −20 mm, after which the error becomes larger. The lever arm mainly affects the contact moment from about 20 mm onwards, while the behaviour is almost the same for lever arms of −10, 0 and +10 mm.

title: Angular error and interaction wrench

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

notes: Next, we vary the centre of compliance between −40, 0 and +40 mm and examine how the angular error, measured force and measured moment change over time. With an opposing centre of compliance, there is no correction at all, while a supporting centre of compliance makes the response approximately one second faster, so the tool becomes flat sooner.

The blue force curve for the supporting configuration is lower during the transient response. This tells us that less pressing force is needed with a supporting centre of compliance, while the forces are equal in the stationary response.

For the opposing centre of compliance, the force is higher because the end effector remains closer to the surface when no alignment occurs. The measured contact force is therefore higher than in the other cases because the end effector is not at the same position.

For the supporting moment, we also notice a response that is about one second faster. The contact moment drops when the tool is almost flat, and the small movement back brings the tool into a completely flat orientation.

Again, less contact moment is needed because of the lever arm and the additional moment it produces. For the opposing configuration, the moment continues to develop until it reaches a stationary value.
This tells us that the moment develops until the tool reaches a certain orientation, without becoming completely flat.

title: Null-space controller

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Rank qualification
text: One null-space direction at full Jacobian rank.

shapes.name: Kinematic preservation
text: Null-space motion preserves the instantaneous motion of the EE.

shapes.name: Conditioning role
text: Adjusts the joint configuration to improve Jacobian conditioning.
At a singularity, the EE loses a motion direction.
Near it, some EE motions require very large joint velocities.

notes: Another study in this work analysed null-space behaviour, and a null-space controller was developed. Our Cartesian pose has six degrees of freedom, while the robot has seven, so one degree of freedom is redundant and allows motion without changing the pose.

We want to eliminate this behaviour, so we introduced two torques. One torque damps this motion, and the other corrects it towards a better configuration, farther from a singularity, by increasing the minimum singular value of the Jacobian.
A singularity is an unfavourable configuration in which the Jacobian loses rank. The robot then cannot move in a particular direction, or would need very high joint velocities to achieve that motion.
[Sources]
MyOwn/chapters/02_theoretical_background.tex
03_software_implementation.tex
04_experimental_setup_and_evaluation.tex. Figure provenance: Final Presentation/figures_and_images/manifest.json.

shapes.name: Null-space finding 1
text: Damping alone reduced cumulative motion by 25.1% compared with no torque.

shapes.name: Null-space finding 2
text: At 2 N m, adding damping to conditioning reduced cumulative motion by 50.7%.

notes: This plot shows four cases while the disturbance is active: no corrective null-space torque, damping torque alone, conditioning torque alone, and the combined damping and conditioning torques. Cumulative joint motion accumulates the magnitude of projected motion using all seven joint velocities. It includes motion in both directions. Without null-space torque, this cumulative motion increases.
With damping, this motion is reduced. Conditioning reduces it further, and the combined torques reduce it even more.

All traces use original t = 5 to 9 s, displayed as t_d = t - 5 s from 0 to 4 s. No null-space torque and damping show a decrease in this indicator. These values describe endpoint changes, not absolute singular values. The larger sample standard deviation at the stronger setting describes variability across the three endpoint changes. title: Conclusion

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Conclusion alignment
text: Compliant rotation allowed contact moments to reduce angular error

shapes.name: Conclusion stiffness
text: Higher rotational stiffness left a larger angular error

shapes.name: Conclusion CoC
text: The CoC could support or oppose the contact moment

shapes.name: Future CoC
text: Use a more rigid tool mount for better measurements

shapes.name: Future return
text: Adapt the CoC to support the contact moment,then return it to the TCP after alignment

shapes.name: Conclusion null-space
text: Null-space control reduced redundant motion under disturbance

notes: To conclude, the contact moment brought the tool flat against the surface when rotational stiffness was compliant. Higher rotational stiffness left a larger angular error, and the centre of compliance could either support or oppose the contact moment.

Finally, the null-space controller opposed the external disturbance affecting the redundant joint motion. Future work could use a more rigid tool mount for better measurements and adaptive centre-of-compliance selection to support the contact moment.
Thank you for your attention.

title: Null-space torques and projector

shapes.name: TextBox 4
text: Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Impedance Controller for a 7-DOF Collaborative Robot

shapes.name: Projector role
text: Projects secondary joint torques into the kinematic null space.

shapes.name: Conditioning role
text: Can act at zero joint velocity.

shapes.name: Direction selector
text: sσ: direction choice, zero in deadband

notes: The kinematic projector selects null-space torque directions. It uses the Jacobian \mboxpseudoinverse J^+.
Damping and conditioning add to give the total null-space torque.
Damping opposes projected joint velocity and is zero at rest. d_null is the damping coefficient.
Conditioning probes both directions along the unit null-space vector v_7. It chooses the direction with the larger minimum singular value.
The selector s_σ is +1 or -1, and zero within the deadband. k_σ sets the torque magnitude, which can be nonzero at rest.
[Sources]
